In this garden, Music Identity pages model the public artist or project names under which music is released or performed.
Naming, person relationships, deduplication and marking follow Logseq/Entity/Identity. A Music Identity is an identity, not a biographical musician.
A recording's Logseq/Frontmatter/created-by-identities lists the identities credited on the release, in published order.
Place releases under the first credited identity as <Identity>/Music/Recording/<Title>, following Logseq/Entity/Music/Recording. A joint release has one page and lists every credited identity.

Place a separately represented composition under its primary credited identity as <Identity>/Music/Work/<Title>, following Logseq/Entity/Music/Work. A recording's artist credit does not establish the composition's authorship.
Personal credits still link the people who actually wrote, produced or performed the music, following Logseq/Entity/Person/Maker.
Bibio and Dorian Concept are solo music identities, each linked to a separate person hub.
Bibio/Music/Recording/Answers credits both identities without creating a separate identity for their collaboration.
In this garden, Band pages model music identities shared by musicians working as a named band.
Attribution and release placement follow Logseq/Entity/Identity/Music, which inherits Logseq/Entity/Identity. A Band instance carries only the Band entity from this lineage.
A band's identity and release namespace persist through changes of membership. Albums belong under the band, rather than under an individual member.

Known people can be linked through Logseq/Entity/Identity/Frontmatter/identity-of. Membership periods, instruments and roles belong in dated body blocks when known; an undated person link makes no claim about current membership.
A recording lists individual participants only when their participation on that recording is known. Neither a current nor a historical membership list establishes a recording credit.
A one-off joint credit is not automatically a band. A named project receives a Band page when it has a band identity of its own.

In this garden, Keyshort pages model a keyboard shortcut: a key, key combination, or key sequence that invokes an action in a particular tool or environment.
An action-specific page under a tool or environment namespace, usually shaped as Scope/Keyshort/Action or Scope/Keyshort/Subscope/Action.
Alternative bindings for the same action may share one page. Closely related actions may share a page when they are reviewed together as a group.
Individual physical or logical keys are Logseq/Entity/Key instances.
A command entered as text is a Logseq/Entity/CLI/Command instance; a Keyshort may invoke that command.
Scope/Keyshort and subscope pages organize shortcuts. Action leaves are the Keyshort instances.
The page name starts with the tool or environment scope, followed by Keyshort and a concise action phrase: Scope/Keyshort/Action.
An optional subscope sits between Keyshort and the action: Scope/Keyshort/Subscope/Action.
The same chord in different scopes represents different Keyshorts because its action and context may differ.
Match the scope and action first, then compare the bindings and descriptions.
Multiple bindings for one action belong on the same page. The same binding for different actions remains separate.
Keyshort pages use the logseq-entity:: property with Logseq/Entity/Keyshort.
A reviewable Keyshort page also includes Logseq/Entity/Card after the Keyshort type in logseq-entity::.
The page carries Keyshort and enough scope links for the relevant {{cards}} queries to find it, either on the review prompt or on a parent block.
A review prompt is marked with . Its child blocks hold the binding and the explanation, so review shows the action before revealing the keys.
Alternative bindings for one action appear as sibling answer blocks beneath the same prompt.
A Keyshort is composed from one or more Logseq/Entity/Key instances.
A Keyshort page may also be a Logseq/Entity/Card when it participates in Logseq review.

In this garden, Mise Task pages model named jobs supplied by a repository or configuration scope and invoked through mise.
A task is identified by its owning repository or configuration collection, config root, and exact task name. Identical names in separate repositories or config roots identify separate tasks.
The task definition can be an executable file or a TOML task. A helper module, package, fixture, or test file becomes part of a task's implementation rather than a separate task entity.
Built-in mise subcommands such as mise run are Logseq/Entity/CLI/Command instances. Jobs invoked through them are Mise Task instances.

Task reference pages belong to the topic served by the job: Topic/mise/Task/<task-name-with-colons-as-slashes>. A namespace prefix already expressed by the topic can be omitted from the page name while remaining in task-name::.

For example, logseq:entity:proxy:page:sync lives at Logseq/Entity/Proxy/Page/mise/Task/sync: the topic already expresses logseq:entity:proxy:page. Repository ownership remains explicit in frontmatter.
If the topic contains distinct implementations of the same task name, add a repository or config-scope segment before the task path. Displayed invocation text retains the exact runnable name.
logseq-entity:: marks the page as a Mise Task instance.
task-owner:: links the owning repository or configuration collection.
task-config-root:: gives the config directory relative to its repository; . denotes the repository root.
task-name:: records the exact local task name, preserving colons and spelling.

source-link:: links the executable file or TOML definition. A review branch or commit link identifies an implementation under review; the repository's default branch identifies the maintained task after it lands.

A portable file task declares task-entrypoint::, task-files::, and any task-dependencies:: in its reference page's frontmatter. These properties let Logseq/Entity/Proxy/Page/mise/Task/sync bring the task's implementation into another garden.
task-entrypoint:: is the executable file's path relative to the source repository root, using forward slashes.

task-files:: is a single-line JSON object mapping each source repository-relative path to its destination graph-relative path. The object lists the entrypoint and every helper, package file, or isolated configuration file needed at runtime. Destination values remain under mise-tasks/. Each path is explicit; wildcards have no meaning.

The entrypoint maps to mise-tasks/<task-name with colons replaced by slashes>. For example, task-name:: logseq:entity:proxy:page:sync maps to mise-tasks/logseq/entity/proxy/page/sync. The imported entrypoint retains its executable mode.

Paths are relative, remain inside their respective roots, and identify regular files. Parent traversal and absolute paths are invalid. A source graph nested inside a repository still uses repository-relative source keys; destination values start at the destination graph root.

task-config-root:: retains the source task's configuration identity. Runtime tools are declared in the file task's mise metadata. A shared runtime configuration or package is transferable when its required files are explicitly mapped under mise-tasks/. Runtime file lookup is relative to the imported entrypoint or its helpers, so the task works after relocation. The destination garden supplies its root mise configuration.

task-dependencies:: is an optional comma-separated list of wikilinks to required Mise Task reference pages. Each dependency supplies its own file mapping, and dependencies are followed recursively with a visited set. A missing task page, invalid declaration, or missing mapped file stops application before writes.

The imported task reference retains task-owner::, task-config-root::, task-name::, and source-link:: from its source identity. Proxy metadata and the destination manifest record where the imported copy came from.

Destination paths shared by tasks must describe the same source file. Conflicting sources claiming one destination path stop application. Previously imported implementation files update when their destination content still matches the last import; a local edit stops application and appears in the preview.
Files removed from the source mapping are reported as cleanup candidates. Re-sync keeps those destination files for review.
A single H1 names the job in plain language. Its first child states what the task accomplishes and when it is useful.
Invocation gives the working directory or repository, the exact command, and one realistic example. Monorepo tasks show their project-qualified invocation.
Inputs and outputs describe required files or arguments, created files and pages, and the result a successful run establishes.
Side effects describes local writes, overwrites, deletion, uploads, and publication when present. Read-only tasks can state their read-only behavior briefly.

Dependencies and access explains tools supplied by mise, Python dependencies supplied by the package manager, platform limits, and credential sources. Version numbers and full argument listings remain in the executable definition, package metadata, and generated help.
Failure and recovery names the failures a reader is likely to meet and the action that resolves each one.
Source and help links the implementation and provides the task's --help invocation. Material behavior changes are reflected in the reference page.
A short task can combine adjacent sections. A task with substantial side effects gives those effects their own section.
Task pages describe one job. Logseq/Entity/Diataxis/How To pages describe a goal and may combine several jobs, editorial decisions, and manual checks.

A how-to links its task reference pages; each task page links relevant how-tos through see-also::. The task reference holds the interface and side effects, while the how-to holds the sequence of actions.
Examples use reusable input paths. Session results and release-specific evidence live on the relevant session pages.
Compare task-owner::, task-config-root::, and task-name:: before creating a task page. The source path supports the match but can change during a refactor.

An alias or monorepo path alias that invokes the same job belongs in the existing task reference. A task rename or implementation move updates the existing reference when the job retains its identity.
In this garden, Movie pages model individual motion-picture works, including documentaries and narrative films.
A released feature film or short film with an identifiable title and release year.
Not this type: a screening event, television series, episode, screenplay, or a page about the general medium of film.
Use Movie/YY/<Title> for a movie, with the four-digit release year when it is known. Preserve the work's official title capitalization.
One page represents one film. Distinguish different works with the same title by year or another clear identity detail.
Record the known release date with date-created::, following Logseq/Date for the date's precision and link form.
Use created-by:: for a filmmaker only when that person has a matching Person hub in the garden.
Begin with an H1 linking the film title to a reliable official or archival page. Add a concise description, director, release year, and useful context or preservation notes when supported by sources.
Search the title, alternate capitalization, director, and release year. Treat remakes and other distinct works as separate movies.

In this garden, Musical Form pages model a named kind of composition that works across composers share, such as the prelude, the nocturne or the fugue, and the structural forms such as ternary or sonata form.
A named kind of piece or structure that more than one composer has written in. The page describes the form itself, apart from any one work.
A named kind of piece and the structure of the same name get sibling pages, Music/Form/Sonata and Music/Form/Sonata Form.
A work's title alone does not make a form: the Morceaux de fantaisie are not fantasias.
A form lives at Music/Form/<Name>, under Music/Form, using its common English name in the singular, as Music/Form/Prelude.

A Logseq/Entity/Music/Work page links each of its forms with music-form::, defined at Logseq/Entity/Music/Work/Frontmatter/music-form. Those links are the form's list of works, so a form page lists works only to add notes about them.
A form page's linked references filtered by a composer's page show that composer's works in the form, since a work page's created-by:: sits in the same frontmatter block as its music-form::.
Start each form page with logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Music/Form]] and one H1 with the form's common name.
Follow with a short description of the form and its history.
Why musical forms get pages of their own, why one Music/Form/ namespace holds both kinds of piece and structures, and why the garden does not model genre.
Forms get their own pages, linked from works

A form page gathers every work in that form across composers. Music/Form/Prelude lists every prelude in the garden in its linked references, and filtering those references by a composer's page narrows the list to that composer's preludes.
Forms get their own pages, linked from works

Each work page links its form with music-form::, defined at Logseq/Entity/Music/Work/Frontmatter/music-form. The filter works because music-form:: and created-by:: sit in the same frontmatter block, so no query is needed.
Forms get their own pages, linked from works
The pattern follows Logseq/Entity/Music/Scale: concept pages under Music/<Concept>/<Name> with an index page above them.
Forms get their own pages, linked from works
One namespace for kinds of piece and structures

"Sonata" names two related things. A sonata is a kind of piece, usually in several movements. Sonata form is the plan of a single movement: exposition, development, recapitulation. The second movement of Beethoven's Pathétique Sonata belongs to a sonata and is a rondo; the first movement of Mozart's Symphony No. 40 is in sonata form and belongs to a symphony.
One namespace for kinds of piece and structures
The two get sibling pages, Music/Form/Sonata and Music/Form/Sonata Form. Musicians already tell them apart that way in speech: "a sonata" and "sonata form."
One namespace for kinds of piece and structures
A name that means one thing in both senses, such as fugue, gets one page.
One namespace for kinds of piece and structures
codekiln finds splitting the sonata from sonata form uncomfortable, and chose the sibling pages because they match how musicians talk.
One namespace for kinds of piece and structures

Alternative: Music/Shape/. "Form" is overloaded and "shape" is not, so Music/Shape/Sonata and Music/Shape/Sonata Form keep the kind of piece apart from the music-theory sense. No one in music uses "shape" this way, so every reader would learn the term from the garden. A nested Music/Shape/Sonata/Form would also imply that sonata form is part of a sonata, which the Mozart example contradicts.
One namespace for kinds of piece and structures

Alternative: Music/Genre/ for kinds of piece, Music/Form/ for structures. Musicologists use "genre" for the symphony, sonata and nocturne: Jim Samson's "Genre" article in Grove Music Online, Jeffrey Kallberg's "The Rhetoric of Genre: Chopin's Nocturne in G Minor" (1988), and Carl Dahlhaus on Gattung. The Library of Congress files "Preludes (Music)" and "Sonatas" among its Genre/Form Terms without choosing between the words. Working musicians call a sonata a form, not a genre, so the split reads as academic jargon.
One namespace for kinds of piece and structures
Genre means different things to different readers: a kind of piece to a musicologist, a style such as rock or ambient to most listeners.

codekiln would model a grouping like genre only if it worked the same way across literature, music and other disciplines of expression, and would prefer a neutral word such as "category." Form may face the same question across disciplines.
Works that organize music history by kinds of piece could change this. Dahlhaus's Nineteenth-Century Music and the Samson article are the places to start.

In this garden, Record Label pages model a label or imprint that releases music recordings.
A record label is the business or imprint named on a release. A label page collects the Logseq/Entity/Music/Recording pages it released.
An imprint with its own name and catalog gets its own page. It links its parent label with part-of:: when that label has a page.
A label that changes its name keeps one page, named for its current name, and its body lists the former names.
A recording studio, distributor, or publisher is a different thing from the label that released a recording.
Place a label at Label/<Name>, using the name printed on its current releases, as Label/Invada Records.

Check the exact page name, alias:: values, former names, the official domain, and plain-text mentions of the label on recording and person pages. A label mentioned only in prose on a recording page gets its page when it is filed.

A recording page links each of its labels with record-label::, defined at Logseq/Entity/Music/Recording/Frontmatter/record-label. Those links are the label's release list, so a label page lists recordings only to add notes about them.
Use founded-by:: for founders with person pages and part-of:: for a parent label.
Start each label page with logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Music/Label]] and one H1 with the label's name, linked to its official site.
Add where the label is based, when it started, its founders, and a source link when known.
